🔍 Three Failed Proofs — testing the mishna's wording for an answer
🐷 A Pig-Like Creature Trailing a Ewe — two opposite rulings from one case
✂️ Plucking Hair Before Slaughtering a Firstborn — Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam's new mishna
🎊 Rav Huna's Festival Dilemma — does plucking count as shearing?

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Nursing, Mercy, and a New Mishna on Firstborns
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 24a–24b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf probes exactly what Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel meant when he said a nursing animal's status 'stands in its presumptive status' — does an animal simply refuse to nurse at all unless it has given birth, or does it refuse to nurse anyone else's young? Three attempts to settle the question from the mishna's own wording are each proposed and dismantled. The stakes surface vividly in Rabbi Yoḥanan's case of a pig-like creature trailing after a ewe, which is simultaneously exempted from firstborn law and forbidden to eat — a combination the Gemara must reconcile, ultimately leaving a related dilemma unresolved. The daf then turns to a new mishna: Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam's method for clearing hair from a firstborn's neck before slaughter without violating the Torah's ban on shearing it, and the parallel question of whether the same technique is permitted on a Festival.

slides.title: 🐑 Does a Mother Nurse Only Her Own Young?
slides.subtitle: Unpacking Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ambiguous phrase

nodes.content: ❓ 'The matter stands in its presumptive status' — presumptive of what, exactly?

columns.label: Reading A
columns.content: An animal won't nurse at all unless it gave birth — but a mother who gave birth MIGHT still nurse another's young

columns.label: Reading B
columns.content: An animal nurses only its OWN young — nursing itself proves certain maternity

nodes.content: ⚖️ The stakes: only Reading B makes slaughtering mother and nursling together a certain violation of 'itself and its offspring' (אוֹתוֹ וְאֶת בְּנוֹ), punishable by lashes
🔍 Three attempts to settle the question from the mishna's own wording — each is proposed and rejected

callout.label: Left open:
callout.text: The Gemara moves on to a new case without ever settling which reading is correct.

slides.title: 🔍 Three Failed Proofs
slides.subtitle: Testing whether the mishna's wording reveals RSbG's true position
rows: The opening ruling: a buyer needn't worry the nursling is another's calf
Doesn't prove certain maternity — either way, the future offspring isn't a firstborn, since nursing at all proves a prior birth
The flock scenario: no concern that first-time and repeat mothers' young were swapped
Even granting that cross-mother mercy is possible in general, a mother with her own young present wouldn't abandon it for another's
'And similarly' (וְכֵן) linking the mishna's two clauses

The clauses describe different scenarios — one with all offspring physically present (certain), one with a single purchased nurser (uncertain); the link refers only to their shared exemption from firstborn status

callout.label: Pattern:
callout.text: Each proof looks compelling until the Gemara finds an alternative reading that removes its force.

slides.title: 🐷 A Pig-Like Creature Trailing a Ewe
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling combines two seemingly opposite conclusions

boxes.title: Exempt From Firstborn Status
items: Follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: an animal nurses only its own young
So the ewe must have already given birth — its next offspring is not a firstborn

boxes.title: Forbidden to Eat
items: Follows the Rabbis: an animal might nurse young that isn't its own — even across species
So the pig-like creature might genuinely be a pig — forbidden 'until Elijah comes and resolves it'

boxes.title: The Resolution
items: Rabbi Yoḥanan is certain the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel throughout the Mishna
What's uncertain: does RSbG's 'mercy' apply only within a species, or across species too?
Aḥai the Distinguished frames the dilemma on both fronts — firstborn status AND permissibility — and it is left standing, unresolved (תֵּיקוּ)

callout.label: Why a pig, not a lamb?
callout.text: A same-species case (ewe nursing a lamb) couldn't test whether mercy crosses species lines — only the pig case can.

slides.title: ✂️ Plucking Hair Before Slaughtering a Firstborn
slides.subtitle: New mishna: Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam solves a conflict between two mitzvot
rows: The Torah forbids shearing a firstborn (Deuteronomy 15:19), yet the neck must be cleared of hair for proper slaughter
Clear space with a cleaver, uprooting hair from both sides of the neck
The plucked hair must not be moved from its place — it stays intermingled so the act doesn't look like deliberate shearing
The same plucking method lets a Sage examine the area for a blemish, to rule on slaughtering the firstborn outside the Temple

callout.label: Underlying principle:
callout.text: An act forbidden in one form (organized shearing) can be permitted when performed differently (incidental plucking for a permitted purpose).

slides.title: 🎊 Rav Huna's Festival Dilemma
slides.subtitle: Does the same plucking technique apply to an ordinary animal slaughtered on a Festival?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav rules: the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam
2️⃣ Question: may one pluck hair the same way from a non-sacred animal's neck before slaughtering it on a Festival (Yom Tov)?
3️⃣ Possibility 1: if 'plucking is not shearing,' then on a Festival it's still forbidden as 'uprooting something from its growth'

4️⃣ Possibility 2: if 'plucking normally IS shearing,' but permitted for the firstborn only as an unintended byproduct of preparing to slaughter, then on a Festival an unintentional act is generally permitted too
5️⃣ Rav Huna defers judgment until Rav Ḥananel confirms Rav's ruling firsthand
6️⃣ Once confirmed, Rav Huna rules: plucking hair before slaughtering an ordinary animal on a Festival is permitted

callout.label: Method:
callout.text: Rav Huna refuses to resolve the Festival question until he is certain what Rav actually said — a case study in careful transmission.

summary.principle: Whether an animal's mercy toward a nursling proves certain maternity remains genuinely unresolved, and the same uncertainty about intention and mechanism shapes both the pig-trailing-a-ewe dilemma and the permitted way to clear a firstborn's neck for slaughter.

flowSteps.content: 🐑 Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's 'presumptive status' phrase admits two readings, with real stakes for lashes
🔍 Three attempts to prove which reading is correct all fail
🐷 The pig-trailing-a-ewe case combines firstborn exemption with forbidden consumption — a related dilemma stands unresolved

columns.content: ✂️ New mishna: plucking, not shearing, clears a firstborn's neck for slaughter
🎊 Rav Huna extends the same technique, cautiously, to Festival slaughter

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Where genuine uncertainty about an animal's or an act's true nature persists, the halakha proceeds carefully rather than resolving the doubt by assumption

quiz.q: According to the Gemara, what is the practical difference between the two readings of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's phrase 'the matter stands in its presumptive status'?
o: Whether the offspring may ever be eaten
Whether one is flogged for slaughtering the mother and nursling together on the same day, under the prohibition against slaughtering an animal and its offspring
Whether the mother animal must be examined for blemishes
There is no practical difference at all
quiz.e: If an animal is merciful only to its own young, the nursling is certainly the mother's offspring, making slaughter of both on the same day a certain violation punishable by lashes; if mercy can extend to others' young, the relationship is uncertain and lashes would not apply.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara reject the proof from the mishna's opening ruling (that a buyer needn't worry the nursling is another's calf)?
o: Because the ruling doesn't actually appear in the mishna
Because either way — whether the nursling is its own or another's — the future offspring isn't a firstborn, since nursing at all proves a prior birth
Because the ruling only applies to gentile sellers
Because Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel later retracted this ruling
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that the mishna's ruling is true regardless of which reading is correct: an animal that nurses at all must have given birth previously, so the future offspring is not a firstborn either way — the wording doesn't prove certain maternity specifically.

quiz.q: In the case of a pig-like creature trailing after a ewe, what does Rabbi Yoḥanan rule about the ewe's firstborn status and about eating the creature?
o: The ewe remains obligated in firstborn law, and the creature is permitted to eat
The ewe is exempt from firstborn law, and the creature is forbidden to eat until Elijah resolves the matter
Both rulings are left completely undetermined
The ewe is exempt, and the creature is definitely non-kosher with no doubt
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan rules the ewe is exempt from having a future offspring counted a firstborn (following Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel), while the pig-like creature itself is forbidden to eat pending a definitive ruling, since it might genuinely be of a forbidden species.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what condition must be met when Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam's method is used to clear hair from a firstborn's neck before slaughter?
o: The hair must be completely removed from the animal
The plucked hair must not be moved from its place, remaining intermingled so it doesn't look like shearing
The hair may only be plucked by a priest
The animal must first be examined by two witnesses
quiz.e: Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam permits clearing space with a cleaver by plucking hair, provided the plucked hair is not moved away — it stays where it fell so the act does not resemble deliberate shearing, which the Torah forbids for a firstborn.

quiz.q: What are the two possible reasons Rav Huna considers for Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam's ruling, and what do they imply for plucking hair on a Festival?
o: Both reasons lead to the same conclusion regardless

If plucking is not shearing, it's still forbidden on a Festival as uprooting growth; if plucking is normally shearing but permitted here as unintentional, then on a Festival an unintentional act is generally allowed
The two reasons only concern the firstborn case and have no bearing on Festivals
Rav Huna rejects both possible reasons
quiz.e: Rav Huna considers that if plucking is fundamentally different from shearing, it should still be forbidden on a Festival as 'uprooting from growth'; but if plucking normally counts as shearing and is permitted for the firstborn only because it's unintentional, then the general Festival leniency for unintentional acts would apply.
